summary: Documents the RC4-HMAC Kerberos encryption types introduced by Microsoft in Windows 2000 as an alternative to the DES-based types, to ease upgrading from Windows NT environments. This RFC is historic.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4757 documents RC4-HMAC encryption types used by Microsoft Windows 2000 with Kerberos. The memo explains how they derive keys and protect messages, and it records security limits that led to a recommendation to use stronger available types.

questions: why did windows 2000 use rc4 for kerberos
what does fortybits mean in kerberos
subtitle: The RC4-based Kerberos encryption and checksum types introduced in Microsoft Windows 2000.

tldr.problem: Windows 2000 needed Kerberos keys that worked with upgraded Windows NT accounts and met the export constraints described in the RFC.
tldr.mechanism: The memo specifies two RC4 encryption types and an HMAC-MD5 checksum type. It derives message keys using a message-type value and uses the NT password hash for compatibility.
tldr.outcome: RFC 4757 is Historic and was updated by RFC 6649. Its security section recommends against these types when stronger alternatives are available and against high-volume use.

today: RFC 4757 is Historic and was updated by RFC 6649. The RFC recommends stronger available encryption types and advises against high-volume use.

sections.title: Why the Types Were Introduced
sections.content:
Windows 2000 introduced new Kerberos encryption and checksum types to support upgrades from Windows NT accounts without DES keying material and to address export restrictions described in the RFC. The document records an existing implementation rather than defining a complete general-purpose Kerberos cryptography system.

The IESG note explains that these types do not provide all operations required by the Kerberos cryptography framework. It also says that this limitation and the security concerns make the specification unsuitable for the standards track.
sections.plainLanguage: The new types let upgraded Windows accounts use Kerberos without first having DES keys. The memo documents those types but says they do not cover every operation in the Kerberos cryptography framework.

sections.title: Password and Message Key Derivation
sections.content:
For compatibility, the RC4-HMAC key is the existing Windows NT password hash. The string-to-key operation applies MD4 to the password encoded as Windows Unicode, with each character represented in little-endian two-octet form and without the terminating zero octets.

Each message type is encoded as a four-octet little-endian integer and contributes to key derivation. The RFC lists distinct values for Kerberos message uses. This separates keying material by message purpose while retaining the account key as the starting point.
sections.plainLanguage: The base key comes from the Windows NT password hash. A value identifying the message type is also used when deriving the key for that message.

sections.title: Checksums and Encryption Types
sections.content:
The checksum type is KERB_CHECKSUM_HMAC_MD5 with value -138. The encryption types are rc4-hmac (23) and rc4-hmac-exp (24). Encrypted data includes a 16-octet checksum and an 8-octet random confounder before the data.

The exportable type uses the string fortybits, a name retained from earlier export limits. In this specification the key size is 56 bits. The full-strength type uses 128-bit keys.
sections.plainLanguage: Each encrypted message includes a checksum and a random confounder. The two registered encryption types use different key strengths, and the exportable type uses a 56-bit key.

sections.title: Security Limits and Status
sections.content:
The RFC warns that RC4 has known weaknesses and recommends against using these types for high-volume connections. It also discusses MD4 weaknesses and notes that no study cited in the document directly proves HMAC-MD4 secure.

The authors recommend using stronger encryption types, such as the AES-based type named in the RFC, when they are available. The unit metadata marks RFC 4757 Historic and records that RFC 6649 updates it.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors describe known concerns with RC4 and MD4. They recommend a stronger available encryption type instead of these types.
